messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: WAIC and hierarchies
parts:
Hi!

Apologies if this has been raised already, but search did not find it: WAIC approximates leave-one-out cross-validation. To be more specific it approximates leave one observation out. However, now assume we have some grouped data, i.e.

y_jk ~ Normal(a_k + b * x_j, sigma)

a_k ~ Normal(mu_a, sigma_a)

Here a_k is a group specific intercept, b a slope and x_j a continuous co-variate. Now, WAIC (as implemented in the R package loo) would compare models by leaving out individual y_jk. But what can be done to compare models on the basis of leave-one-group out? That is, I would like to assess if the model can predict groups well (and not just single observations). The problem is that groups can be unbalanced, i.e. some groups may have in realty more observations than others.

So what to do in this situation or is this question not meaningful in a WAIC type approach?

Bonus question: In the linear case the likelihood for a group is analytically tractable (albeit I am not sure about what to do about the scaling of the log-lik with the number of data items), but how about cases where this is lost like logistic regression?

Best,
Sebastian

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: WAIC and hierarchies
parts:
WAIC and importance-sampling LOO work well if the full posterior and leave-one-out posterior are close together, or in other words if a single observation is not highly influential. It's possible to use LOO and WAIC for groups, but it's likely that the group of observations is highly influential and the full posterior and leave-one-group-out posterior are too different, and the distribution of the importance ratios has too high variance to get useful results. Figure 11 in Vehtari & Lampinen (2002) http://becs.aalto.fi/en/research/bayes/publications/VehtariLampinen_NC2002_preprint.pdf shows an example where the performance of the importance sampling approximation is bad for leave-one-group-out. Although computation in WAIC is different than in importance sampling, it has similar behavior to IS-LOO (expect with lower variance and higher bias due to the truncation in the Taylor series approximation). We'll post soon more results on IS-LOO and WAIC.

I would recommend computing the leave-one-group-out in brute-force way, or if there are too many groups then in k-fold-CV way. You could also test importance-sampling leave-one-group-out using very good importance sampling <http://arxiv.org/abs/1507.02646>, which would also warn you if it's not going to work.

Aki

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] WAIC and hierarchies
parts:
Hi, we discuss the topic in this paper:
http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf
The short answer is that I think any general Stan implementation will have to be one data point at a time, but in any particular application you can cross-validate by groups.
A
